name: Asahel Pierce's Blacksmith Shop

placement.symbolic_location: Lake Street at the corner of Canal Street (historically Lake and West Water), west side, one block west of the river — modelled on the SOUTH-EAST corner. Which of the four corners is not attested.

construction.note: THAT IT WAS BUILT OF SAWN LUMBER IS DOCUMENTED BY IMPLICATION AND THE REST IS THE ARCHETYPE'S. Andreas: 'Being unable to find suitable lumber in Chicago, he was obliged to haul his material from Plainfield, forty miles' — a man does not haul boards forty miles by ox team to build a log pen, so the shop was a board building and not log, which is a genuine finding and the reason this record uses outbuilding rather than log_dwelling. WHICH WAY THE BOARDS WENT IS NOT ATTESTED: `light_frame` is the archetype's term for boards laid horizontally on a stick frame and `plank` for boards nailed on vertically, and nothing chooses between them here. The horizontal reading is taken because it is the more finished of the two and this was a shop on the town's main street rather than a field shelter. That last step is a preference.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 3.0 m is about 10 ft at the eave: headroom to swing a sledge and to stand a horse under, with air over a forge. Stated rather than left to the archetype's size-aware default of 3.14 m for this footprint, which is close enough that the difference is not the point — the point is that the number is the record's and its reasoning is on the record.

door.note: No source describes an opening. 'stable' is the archetype's 1.35 m clear doorway, sized for a horse led through in hand, and shoeing is half of what a frontier smith did. The wider 'wagon' opening is tempting because Pierce ironed wagons and stage gear, but that work is done to the ironwork rather than to the assembled vehicle, and a 2.9 m opening would need a taller wall than this record claims.

forge.note: STATED AND NOT BUILT, AND IT IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE BUILDING. Andreas records that Pierce bought the Rev. Mr See's old set of tools and set up in business, that he ironed the first Chicago-to-St-Louis stage line in January 1834 and that he began making the 'Bull' plough in the spring — none of which is possible without a forge, a bellows and a stack to take the smoke. The outbuilding archetype has no chimney parameter and no interior, so the mesh shows a shed with a doorway and NO SMOKE, which is the one feature of a smithy anybody in the street would have noticed. Nothing about the forge's size, position or the stack's material is attested in any case. Owed an admission in docs/LIBERTIES.md.

function.note: A blacksmith shop from October 1833, doing the ironwork the town and the road trade needed: Andreas records the order from John T. Temple & Co. for 'doing the ironing for the first stage line between Chicago and St. Louis' in January 1834, and the manufacture of the old-fashioned 'Bull' plough with a wooden mould-board from the spring of 1834 (scan p. 1161). THAT PLOUGH IS THE REASON THIS BUILDING MATTERS BEYOND ITS OWN CORNER: it is the wet-prairie tool, and a smith on the west side making them is the town's agricultural hinterland arriving in the town. Whether he was making them on 1835-07-01 specifically is not attested.

occupants.note: Named as the builder and proprietor, arriving from Vermont on 8 October 1833 (scan p. 1161). Andreas gives his later Chicago career — alderman in 1843 and 1844, and two streets named after him (scan pp. 387, 411) — which corroborates the man and says nothing about who was at the anvil in July 1835.

citations.citation: Andreas, A. T. History of Chicago: From the Earliest Period to the Present Time. Vol. 1. Chicago: A. T. Andreas, 1884.

research_note: NOT ON THE PARCEL'S ORIGINAL LIST AND ADDED ON THE EVIDENCE. The task that produced this parcel asked whether Matthias Mason & Co., blacksmiths, could be placed from the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833; they cannot — the advertisement gives no address, and inventing one would put a named smithy at a false corner. A full-text search of Andreas turned up a better answer three lines below the brickyard passage: a smithy at a DOCUMENTED junction, with a documented date, a documented reason for its construction method, and two documented pieces of work, on the west side in this parcel's own ground. So the town gets its working smithy from the evidence rather than from a guess. TWO CAUTIONS. First, do not merge this with blacksmith_shop_state_st, the shop attested near the Agency House at the foot of State Street on the north side (Andreas scan p. 1161 also) — they are different buildings on opposite sides of the town, and this dataset carries both. Second, do not attach Mason's name to either: nothing connects the Democrat's advertiser to either shop, and the identification would be an invention wearing a citation. WHAT WOULD UPGRADE THIS RECORD: any statement of which corner, which is the one real gap in an otherwise unusually well-attested small building; and further issues of the Chicago Democrat, whose advertising columns are where a smith says where his shop is.
